solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Piece of hair cut at an angle requires this (4)

definitions.text: cut at an angle requires this

blocks.note: read as a strand the barber is working on: a curl or tress

blocks.clueFragment: cut at an angle requires this
blocks.note: read again as waterways: in Britain a cut is a man-made canal, and one running up a slope needs a gated chamber to lift boats

explanation.surface: A hairdresser explains that an angled cut needs a particular strand to work with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' reads as a haircut, which the first half encourages; it is a canal, and a canal climbing an incline must be fitted with locks.
explanation.definitionFit: A lock of hair is a tress; a canal lock is the gated chamber that carries a cut up or down a gradient: one word, two trades.

clue.text: Coral reefs with no resistance to change look less good (4,4)

indicators.note: 'with no X' means X is absent, so a letter is taken out of the fodder
letters that change are rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: the raw fodder, ten letters
R is the physics symbol for resistance; one R is removed, leaving COALEEFS

explanation.surface: Reefs that lose their resilience to environmental change end up looking shabbier.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one of the two Rs in 'coral reefs' goes; the surface's talk of resistance to change sounds like ecology but is two separate instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom borrowed from Chinese: to lose face is to suffer a loss of standing, to look worse in others' eyes.

clue.text: The King having his investiture? (8)

blocks.note: CR = Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles
having = possessing

explanation.surface: A question about whether the monarch is about to be formally installed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a description of a coronation, and the wordplay is tucked inside it: the King's Latin initials, then a synonym for 'having'.
explanation.definitionFit: Investiture is formal installation in office, and for a monarch that ceremony is the placing of the crown.

clue.text: Turned up again outside wine bars (10)

indicators.note: to bar is to shut in behind bars, so the wine encloses the other piece

blocks.note: red wine; it opens round the next piece
the outside of a thing is its surface

explanation.surface: Someone reappears in front of the local wine bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wine bars' looks like one noun, but 'bars' is the verb, and 'outside' seems a position word when it is really an ingredient.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from a diver or submarine coming back up: whatever has resurfaced has turned up again after going missing.

clue.text: Sullen nuisance displaying listlessness and dissatisfaction (5)

indicators.note: to display is to put on show, so the answer is visible inside the words before it

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: A moody pest showing boredom and discontent.
explanation.walkthrough: A French word taken into English. The definition is long because the answer blends two ideas, weariness and discontent.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is French for boredom, a weary listlessness born of dissatisfaction with one's lot.

clue.text: Prepared to fight, subject to members’ control (5,4)

blocks.note: read as soldiers mustered, equipped and ready for battle
read again as anatomy: a member is a limb, so this is what sits beneath the limbs

explanation.surface: Soldiers mobilised, but only under the direction of a parliament's members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' suggests politicians or a club, but a member is also a limb; the answer read as one word is the armpits.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops under arms are mobilised for battle, and the underarms are the parts beneath one's arms, which are limbs or members.

clue.text: State where ignorance is bliss? (5,8)

blocks.note: read as a nation on the map, and meant as a condition of mind
the proverb: happiness that holds only as long as you do not know the facts

explanation.surface: A riddle about a country where not knowing makes people happy.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart: the question mark flags that the geography is a joke, and the proverb 'ignorance is bliss' names the condition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a happiness built on delusion, which is exactly what 'ignorance is bliss' describes.

clue.text: Head of cage bird that’s black [and] yellow (6)

indicators.note: the head of a thing is its top, so the first letter of the next word

blocks.note: first letter of cage
the large crow whose plumage is entirely black

explanation.surface: A description of a caged bird with black and yellow plumage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black and yellow' reads as a colour scheme, but yellow means cowardly here.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is slang for cowardly, and craven is the older literary word for the same failing.

clue.text: Duke and bishop filled with fear [in] tower (6)

indicators.note: something filled with X has X inside it, so the bishop's letters take the next piece in

blocks.note: D = duke
RR = Right Reverend, a bishop's title
awe = dread; goes between the two Rs

explanation.surface: A duke and a bishop trapped in a tower, terrified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tower' is not a building but one who tows, and hauling a load along is drawing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower is one who tows, and to draw a cart is to pull it, so one who draws is the same thing.

clue.text: Military commander pierced by tip of this weapon (7)

indicators.note: a thing pierced has something pushed into it, so a letter goes inside the commander
the tip is the point at the very end of an object, here the first letter of 'this'

blocks.note: the hereditary military ruler of feudal Japan
first letter of this; goes inside SHOGUN

explanation.surface: A general stabbed by the point of the very weapon being described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This weapon' seems to point back at the commander's own sword; 'this' is only a word lending its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a shotgun is a smooth-bored firearm, one kind of weapon.

clue.text: Senior officer’s way of getting around mass protest (7,6)

blocks.note: an army officer of top rank, with the possessive S
a tricycle, a means of transport

explanation.surface: How a high-ranking officer circumvents a large demonstration.
explanation.walkthrough: The break between the pieces falls one letter away from the break in the answer. 'Getting around' reads as dodging the protest but means travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A general strike is a stoppage across all trades at once, a protest made by the mass of workers; Britain had one in 1926.

clue.text: Small-scale scene I love in theatre (7)

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: I as written
love = zero in tennis scoring = O; follows I
theatre = drama; wraps round IO after its first letter

explanation.surface: A playgoer declaring their love for the miniature set in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatre' seems to be where the speaker is standing; it is the container, and the scene's theatrical flavour hides that the definition is a model.
explanation.definitionFit: A diorama is a three-dimensional model of a scene, often in a museum case, so a scene built to a small scale.

clue.text: Person with money wearing more elaborate clothes (9)

indicators.note: read as a verb: to clothe something is to wrap it, so the second piece goes round the first

blocks.note: someone in a coat is wearing it
fancier = more ornate; wraps round IN after its first letter

explanation.surface: A rich person dressed more showily than anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' is the trap: it looks like a noun going with 'wearing', but it is a verb saying which piece wraps which.
explanation.definitionFit: A financier manages or supplies large sums, so is a person defined by money.

clue.text: Britpop band rocked on the radio (5)

indicators.note: radio is heard, not read, so go by sound

blocks.note: rocked = moved to and fro

explanation.surface: A 1990s British band played a rock set on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Britpop was the 1990s wave of guitar bands from Britain. 'Rocked' wants to mean played loud music; it means moved to and fro.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Suede were a London band who helped launch the Britpop scene in the early 1990s.

clue.text: This part of magazine could be recent (6,6)

definitions.text: This part of magazine could be recent

blocks.note: read as a section of the paper, and meant literally as a place in it: the middle pages
read as up to date, and meant as a word whose six letters, scattered about, could become 'recent'

explanation.surface: A remark that one section of a magazine might be up to date.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is itself an instruction: the middle word, its letters spread about, makes 'recent'. The solver works backwards from the result to the recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: The centre spread is the pair of facing pages in the middle of a magazine, and read as a recipe it scatters CENTRE into RECENT.

clue.text: Artists in a funny way capturing lives? (9)

definitions.text: Artists in a funny way capturing lives?

indicators.note: funny can mean odd, so the letters are put in an odd order
what is captured is held inside, so the scrambled letters hold the next piece

blocks.note: anagram fodder
she lives = she is, existing; held within the rearranged letters

explanation.surface: A definition of writers who portray people's lives comically.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines the answer, which is why the question mark is there: these are artists who capture lives in a funny way.
explanation.definitionFit: Satirists are writers and cartoonists who depict people and their doings with mocking humour.

clue.text: Small interval recalled by individual (8)

indicators.note: called back, so the word before it runs backwards

blocks.note: by = times, as in 'three by four'; turned round
individual = one

explanation.surface: A brief pause remembered by one person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like a link word joining the halves, but in arithmetic it means multiplied by. In music this is the step between adjacent keys on a piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical interval is the gap between two notes, and the semitone is the smallest one in Western tuning.

clue.text: Seats get vandalised [in] flats and properties (5,3)

indicators.note: vandalised things are wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Seating in blocks of flats and other buildings gets smashed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flats and properties' reads as housing; in the theatre flats are painted scenery panels and properties are props.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition in theatre jargon: scenery flats and props together make up what stands on the stage for a production.

clue.text: Epic historical work [is] somewhat over-the-top (3,9)

blocks.note: read as a sweeping saga or chronicle, and meant as a scripture of kings, wars and migrations
over-the-top is abbreviated OTT; take only some of it, the first two letters

explanation.surface: A reviewer calls a sweeping historical saga a bit excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay yields an abbreviation, not letters: OT, part of OTT, is the standard short form of the answer, as in Bible references.
explanation.definitionFit: The first part of the Christian Bible is a vast narrative history of ancient Israel, epic in scale.

clue.text: Tell family member to avoid Roman square (6)

indicators.note: to avoid something is to stay clear of it, so the square is dropped

blocks.note: a kinsman or kinswoman
IV is Roman 4, a square number; removed from RELATIVE

explanation.surface: Advice to warn a relative to keep away from a piazza in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman square' pictures a piazza; it is a square number written in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the storytelling sense: to relate events is to recount or tell them.

clue.text: Support for young boxer? (4,2)

blocks.note: pro = in favour of
a boxer is a dog breed, and a young dog is a pup

explanation.surface: Backing for a promising teenage fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' pictures a fighter, but the question mark signals the dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb comes from shoring up with a prop, a post that bears weight, so it means to support.

clue.text: One likely to wade in after getting pushed around (5)

definitions.text: One likely to wade in after getting pushed around

blocks.note: read as someone quick to join a fight, and meant as a bird that walks into shallow water
read as being bullied first; the bird is pushed along by nothing but its own long legs

explanation.surface: Someone who joins a fight once they have been shoved about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wade in' suggests piling into a scrap; the answer wades literally, a small white heron hunting in shallows.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by habit: egrets are herons that wade in shallow water to hunt fish and frogs.

clue.text: Making good broadcast on a revolutionary (9)

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another comes after it
a revolution is a turn, so the word before it is turned round

blocks.note: a = per, as in 'twice a day'; turned round
a showing on radio or television

explanation.surface: A political insurgent being rehabilitated in a radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' pictures a rebel; here it only says the tiny word before it turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good damage is an idiom for mending it, and 'making good' is the -ing form to match.

clue.text: Petty officer fences stolen picture (5)

indicators.note: to fence something in is to enclose it

blocks.note: PO = petty officer, a naval rank
hot = stolen; goes inside PO

explanation.surface: A naval officer acts as receiver for a stolen painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fences' reads as dealing in stolen goods, which the surface supports; it means encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: A short form of photograph, a picture taken with a camera.

clue.text: ChatGPT possibly invents things [and] is relevant (7)

blocks.note: ChatGPT is one example of a software application
invents things = tells falsehoods

explanation.surface: A jibe that the chatbot makes things up but still has its uses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks ChatGPT as an example of something, here the kind of program on a phone.
explanation.definitionFit: A rule that bears on a case is said to apply to it, so the verb in the third person means is relevant.

clue.text: Old despot from America [is] difficult to deal with (7)

blocks.note: O = old
the tyrant emperor of Rome
US = United States

explanation.surface: An ageing American dictator proves hard to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old despot' looks like a single idea, but 'Old' gives its own letter before the emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin onus, a burden: an onerous duty weighs on you and is hard to deal with.

clue.text: Countenance / particular means of communicating (10)

blocks.note: read as the look on a face
read as a set phrase or idiom, one particular way of putting something

explanation.surface: A face, and a special way of getting a message across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Countenance' can also be a verb meaning tolerate, which leads nowhere; it is the noun for a face.
explanation.definitionFit: A countenance is a facial look, and a turn of phrase is also called by the same word: one noun, two senses.

clue.text: Criminal / tendency (4)

blocks.note: read as British slang for corrupt, as of a police officer on the take
read as a natural inclination or aptitude

explanation.surface: A crook and his leanings.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a crooked policeman is a bent copper; the other sense is the one in 'a bent for music'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses grow from not straight: crooked in conduct, or leaning one way by nature.
